data.title: The Church of St Margaret of Antioch at Kopčany – the oldest standing building in Slovakia
data.excerpt: The Church of St Margaret of Antioch stands outside the village of Kopčany, on the left bank of the River Morava, and is regarded as the oldest standing ecclesiastical building in Central Europe. Graves of the 9th to the early 10th century found beside it in 2004 date its construction to the time when the Great Moravian hillfort of Valy at Mikulčice was built.
data.metaTitle: St Margaret at Kopčany – the oldest standing church
data.metaDescription: The Church of St Margaret of Antioch at Kopčany is regarded as the oldest standing church in Central Europe. Great Moravian graves date it to the 9th century.

children.text: The Church of St Margaret of Antioch stands in the village of Kopčany, Skalica district. It stands outside the village on the left bank of the River Morava. It served as a parish church (first mentioned in 1392) until the 18th century. It is regarded as the oldest standing ecclesiastical building in Central Europe. It was built in connection with the construction of the Great Moravian hillfort of Valy at Mikulčice, at the latest in the 9th century.

blocks.alt: The Church of St Margaret of Antioch – the oldest standing building in Slovakia

children.text: Slovaks can be rightly proud of this unique church. It is, after all, the only building from the period of Great Moravia that still stands and survives. No such building exists in the Czech Republic or anywhere else. At the same time it should be realised that this inconspicuous little church is practically the oldest surviving standing building north of the Danube, which gives it enormous importance for the whole of Central Europe as well. The little church is at the same time living proof of how nonsensical it is to understand the borders of Moravia and Nitrava according to today's borders of Slovakia and the Czech Republic. Kopčany formed part of Mikulčice, which the Moravians claim for themselves. In reality, however, the hillfort of Valy itself lay directly on the River Morava, on an island, or rather on several islands. Only in a later period, after the demise of the hillfort, did the Morava gradually change its channel into its present state. According to the present understanding of borders, which follow the River Morava, it could therefore be said that Mikulčice was half Slovak and half Moravian, which is of course nonsense. The Moravia of the 9th century (by which I mean the original “Mojmír's” Moravia) undoubtedly included a large part of western Slovakia as well. It is out of the question that the power centre of Moravia should lie on the border of the principality. Such centres lay as a rule deep in the interior. After the incorporation of western Slovakia into the Kingdom of Hungary, the eastern part of Moravia (above all today's Záhorie) gradually ceased to identify itself with the original Moravia, and the name remained only for its western part. It is a paradox, however, that precisely that part of today's Moravia which formed the centre of historical Moravia is still called Slovácko, which evokes various associations.

children.text: The first known conventional archaeological excavation of the cemetery beside the Church of St Margaret at Kopčany was carried out in 1961 by Ľ. Kraskovská. Among the skeletons uncovered in a strip trench north of the church she found no finds that would allow them to be dated, and she considered the church itself to be Early Gothic. V. Drahošová returned to the investigation of the cemetery and the church in 1994–1996. With four trenches around the perimeter of the church and one in the interior she again recorded inhumation graves without any grave goods at all, and west of the church, in trench 2/94/95, fragments of older masonry later identified as the foundations of a narthex. The year 1998 can be regarded as a fundamental turning point, when the Monuments Board of the Slovak Republic began to carry out a systematic archaeological investigation of the whole cadastral area of Kopčany. In 2004 P. Baxa discovered beside the Church of St Margaret graves of the 9th to the early 10th century, which date the origin of the church to the Great Moravian period.

Its age is also attested by the walls, which are not vertical but curve archaically inwards towards the top. The building underwent its first more marked alterations around the middle of the 13th century, when the original semicircular-headed windows of the nave were modified. On the northern side they were walled up, and on the southern side they were changed into the form of Early Gothic windows with stone mullions. A similar window was also cut through in the southern wall of the apse. In the second half of the 16th century the original entrance on the western side of the nave was replaced by a larger Gothic portal, set asymmetrically. This was probably connected with the construction of a gallery in the western part of the nave. In addition, the little church received a new altar. In the 17th century the windows were altered, which concerns above all the window on the southern side of the nave, the one closer to the apse, which was replaced by a large Baroque window opening in the shape of a semicircle. In this century the occupation around the little church came to a definitive end, and it was left alone in a marshy landscape. Thanks to the care of the faithful, however, it did not perish. It was last repaired as long ago as 1926.

children.text: In conclusion it should be added that the most recent research suggests that at least one more building stands in Slovakia whose origin reaches back to the period of Great Moravia, namely the little church in the village of Kostoľany pod Tribečom. The Great Moravian origin of the church at Kostoľany is so far attested only dendrochronologically, when analysis of a wooden beam from the wall showed that it most probably comes from a tree felled around the year 860. It should be added that this church was dated indirectly to the 9th century on the basis of the find of structural timber in the masonry not only dendrochronologically but also by measuring the content of C14 carbon. By this method too the wood is dated to the course of the 9th century. This is important, because if certain objections can be raised against the dendro-dating concerning the lower degree of conclusiveness of the tree-ring sequence established, then a completely identical dating by another method must dispel these doubts. The only thing that Kostoľany so far lacks in comparison with Kopčany are Great Moravian graves respecting the structure of the church. Their absence is the only reason why historians do not yet dare to assign Kostoľany to the Great Moravian period.

children.text: In closing I add an interesting article from the website devoted to the hillfort at Mikulčice (http://www.mikulcice-valy.info/default.asp?cont=113) – a quotation from the architectural and urban-planning study which was publicly presented at Mikulčice on 28 June 2006, which shows what importance is attributed to this little church, inconspicuous at first sight:

blocks.text:
Proposal for the presentation of the Church of St Margaret of Antioch

The manner of presenting the Great Moravian church is at present at the stage of research. Given the established philosophy of the archaeological park, it is possible on the one hand to propose some methods of presentation definitively, but on the other hand only to anticipate others.In view of the present state of research it is possible to settle the view on the presentation of those parts of the architecture of the Great Moravian church that lie below ground. These are parts of the foundation masonry of the narthex with the walled feature of a pit. In the context of the proposed correction of the presentation of the replicas of the church masonry within the Great Moravian hillfort of Valy, it is proposed here to display the narthex over the whole extent of the ground plan of the narthex. The foundation would be built up (as on the Czech side) to a height of about 25 cm in quarried stone. The pit feature will be covered with a stone slab, and the inner part of the narthex will be filled with sand or good gravel¨.The above-ground masonry of the church has to be understood in the context of all the building alterations through which the church has passed. The main overall method of conservation is the maximum presentation of the early medieval occupation layer. A method of conservation has recently been carried out which, by an analytical method, also presents the later phases of the building. It is assumed that if the building is to be presented in its Great Moravian character, the effect of the other interventions will have to be limited. The presentation of the medieval analytical trenches will have to be suppressed both in time and in structure.If a roof from the fourth – Baroque – building phase is accepted within the presentation, then in the longer term it will be necessary to plan the replacement of the present roofing with extruded ceramic tiles with a pointed end, typical of this region at least since the 19th century, if not rather earlier.

Proposal for the presentation of the cemetery Given the fact that there is not enough information about the site of the cemetery, the presentation of the cemetery would be minimised and would consist in placing the surviving gravestone in the south-western part of the area, opposite the end of the adjoining educational trail in the northern part of the site. The area around the church is, like the rest of the archaeological park, laid to grass. The space in front of the western front of the church is open and is understood as an assembly area in front of the church, used at the times when occasional services are held.

Functional use of the site Within the functional use of the site, the holding of services of an intimate character inside the church is envisaged. For the purposes of the services, a utility annexe in the grounds of the Kačenárna is proposed as facilities for the priest, Besides a sacristy, a store for occasional furniture for the services is also envisaged there.In the case of services in the open air, the placing of a portable altar on the restored narthex is envisaged. The faithful would gather in front of the western front of the church. These services are connected with the pilgrimage.

Infrastructure At the church an underground supply of electrical cabling can be envisaged, which will also have to be brought into the grounds of the Kačenárna.With the connection of electric current it would be possible to consider lighting the church both inside and outside.
